name: Low Earth Orbit
description: 500 km up, circles Earth every 95 minutes. Close = sharp images and cheap launches. But you only see a ground station for a few minutes per pass, you spend 36 min of every orbit in Earth's shadow, and thin air slowly drags you down, so you need fuel to stay up and to deorbit at the end (space-debris rule).
cons: Drag needs fuel to stay up
Must deorbit at end of life

name: Sun-Synchronous Orbit
description: A polar orbit tilted so you pass over every place at the same local time: perfect lighting for comparing images over months. Passes over polar ground stations often. Needs fuel to deorbit at end of life.
pros: Same lighting every pass — perfect for comparing images
Frequent passes over polar ground stations
cons: Needs about 150 m/s to deorbit at end of life
Eclipse every orbit — needs a battery
Short contact with a single mid-latitude station

name: Geostationary Orbit
description: 35,786 km up; one orbit takes exactly one day, so you hover over the same spot — continuous weather watching and 24-hour contact with one station. Far away: blurry for small details, weaker radio signal, the rocket drops you in a transfer orbit and your spacecraft must burn 1,500 m/s to circularize.
pros: Stares at one region all the time
cons: Far = blurry details and weaker signal
Spacecraft must burn 1,500 m/s to circularize

name: Low Lunar Polar Orbit
description: 100 km over the Moon's poles: maps the whole surface, including dark craters near the poles. Needs a deep-space antenna network; the Moon's lumpy gravity disturbs the orbit, so station-keeping fuel is high; no magnetic field, so magnetorquers do not work.
pros: Maps the entire Moon including polar craters
cons: Lumpy lunar gravity costs 100 m/s per year

name: Sun-Earth L2 Halo Orbit
description: 1.5 million km from Earth on the side away from the Sun. The Sun, Earth and Moon are always behind you, so a telescope stays cold and steady with no eclipses. Far: deep-space network required, limited contact hours. The orbit is unstable, so small corrections are needed.
pros: Cold, stable, no eclipses — ideal for telescopes
Sun and Earth always behind you
cons: 1.5 million km away — deep-space network required

name: Mars Polar Orbit
description: Sunlight at Mars is only 43% as strong, so solar arrays must be larger. Radio signals take minutes to arrive (average 12.5 min one way), so the spacecraft must handle emergencies on its own. Getting there takes ~7 months and Mars launch windows open only every 26 months.
